newsitem.title: GREECE: Farmers march in Athens, PM turns down demands.
newsitem.headline: Farmers march in Athens, PM turns down demands.

text.p: Thousands of angry farmers marched through Athens on Thursday to push their costly demands on the socialist government but Greek Prime Minister Costas Simitis said he would quit before giving in.

More than 7,000 farmers descended on the Greek capital in a convoy of buses and trucks from agricultural regions in Thrace, Thessaly and Macedonia. They were joined in Athens for a march on parliament by students and construction workers.
Beating drums and chanting anti-government slogans, farmers paraded a truckload of sheep in front of the agriculture ministry before starting their march.
It was one of the largest rallies so far in a campaign by farmers, public workers, seamen, teachers, pensioners and others against Simitis's economic reform policies.
"We will break their Thatcherite tactics. We know they want to divide and crack us so they can pass even meaner measures," said Vangelis Boutos, one of the farmers' leaders.
Thousands of farmers have blocked national roads for 22 days with an army of tractors, causing transport chaos and inflicting more than $100 million in damage on the economy.
They want lower fuel prices, higher price supports and $1.3 billion in debts rescheduled but Simitis has said the state has no more money to give to farmers or anyone else.

Many barricades have come down in recent days and farmers in some regions have lost heart but blockades on the north-south motorway in the Thessaly region have stayed in place, virtually cutting the country in two.
The farmers want direct talks with Simitis to explain their problems but the prime minister slammed the door on them again on Thursday, refusing to meet them while roads were blocked.
In an interview published on Thursday in Nitro magazine, he stood by his firm rejection of concessions for farmers or other workers who have staged protests against his economic policies.
"I'd rather go home," Simitis told Nitro when asked if he would yield to protesters.
"My job is to spread the existing money in a socially just way and that is why we must fight not to succumb to blackmail," Simitis, a frosty economics' professor, said.
Simitis, facing his first crisis since winning elections in September, has flatly rejected the farmers' demands, saying the 1997 budget could not afford the $4 billion cost.
The farmers' march coincides with a debate in parliament on the 1997 budget, which ends on Saturday night with a vote which Simitis should win easily.

The budget has triggered a wave of strikes and protests in recent weeks by an array of unhappy groups who oppose Simitis's mix of tight incomes, higher direct and indirect taxes and the abolition of hundreds of tax exemptions.
Simitis has said that fiscal rigour is necessary for Greece's priority of meeting European Union economic targets. He has said that sacrifices must be made, especially by the wealthy.
